summary: This unit teaches you to buy what a fabrication job needs: steel, consumables, gases, services such as galvanising, and equipment. You will learn to write a full specification, get and compare quotations fairly, negotiate honestly, raise an approved purchase order, import goods when they are not sold locally, follow up and receive the order, deal with faults, pay correctly and judge how well each supplier performs, with the calculations a buyer uses at each step.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you learned to order materials for a job you were working on. At Level 3 you take charge of **purchasing**: you decide exactly what is bought, from whom and on what terms, and you must be able to show that the money was spent fairly and well.

Good buying keeps a job on time and on budget. Poor buying shows up as the wrong grade of steel, plate that arrives a week late, a galvanised frame that burst in the bath, an import held at the port, or a cheap quote that turned out dearer than the rest. Most of these faults start with a vague specification or a skipped step.

**Who it is for:** Level 3 welders and fabricators, team leaders and anyone who buys for a fabrication shop or a training centre workshop. The examples use private shops and the Centre, which is a public body and must follow the procurement rules for public bodies.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan purchases from the job's needs
Turn drawings, cutting lists and the programme into approved requisitions, with the date each item is needed.
Grade and standard, sizes, finish, quantity, certificates, packaging and delivery, agreed with the supervisor or engineer.
Send the same request for quotation (RFQ) to approved suppliers; compare total cost; score them with weights agreed in advance.
Negotiate fairly; raise a numbered purchase order within the approval limits, with the right contract terms.
Specify the work and the checks for services such as galvanising and laser cutting; compare whole-life cost for machines.
Work out the landed cost in J$, understand FOB and CIF, gather the documents, plan the timeline and manage the risks.
Expedite the order, check what arrives against the order and certificates, deal with rejects, match the invoice and pay on the right terms.
Keep prices confidential, declare conflicts of interest, never split orders, keep records an auditor can follow, and review supplier performance.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on specifying, quotations, ethics, supplier choice, importing, calculations, stock planning, ways of buying, following up, services, equipment, problems and payment.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as FOB, CIF, EOQ, tender, validity and packing list, and short calculations) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals:** a role play in which you write a specification and RFQ, score the quotes on a weighted sheet, negotiate and raise a recommended purchase order; and an import plan in which you work out the landed cost, draw a timeline, list the documents and risks, compare with a local price and present the plan to the manager.

blocks.note: Bring a calculator to every lesson. Many marks come from simple sums done carefully: percentages, kilograms and tonnes, exchange rates, weighted scores and discounts. Write each step down and ask yourself whether the answer makes sense.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Purchasing is a chain of steps, each with an owner and a record. If one link is missing, money is wasted, the wrong steel arrives, or nobody can show later why a supplier was chosen.

flow: Need: the supervisor or estimator works out what the job needs from the drawings, cutting list and programme
Requisition: a written request to buy, approved by the person who controls the job's budget
Specification: the buyer and the supervisor or engineer describe exactly what is needed
Request for quotation (RFQ), or a tender for large public purchases, sent to approved suppliers
Evaluation: quotes brought to the same basis and scored against criteria agreed beforehand
Negotiation: a fair, recorded discussion with the best one or two suppliers
Purchase order (PO): numbered, approved within the spending limits, sent to the supplier
Expediting: the order is confirmed and chased before the due date
Receiving: the storekeeper checks goods and certificates against the PO and records them
Payment: accounts match the invoice with the PO and the receipt, then pay on the agreed terms
Review: the supplier's performance is recorded and all papers are filed with the job

head: Document
Who raises it
What it does
rows: Asks for goods to be bought: job number, items, quantity, date needed. Approved by the budget holder.
Asks suppliers to price the same specification by the same closing date.
Price, delivery time, terms and how long the price holds (its validity).
The firm's numbered order: specification, quantity, price, delivery, terms. Once the supplier accepts it, it is a contract.
Confirms the order. Check it matches the PO line by line.
What was sent, and what is in each bundle or crate.
What actually arrived, and in what condition.
The bill for the goods or service.
Tells the supplier that the buyer is reducing what it owes, for example for goods returned, short or overcharged.
The supplier's own document reducing the amount the buyer owes.

blocks.note: **Three-way match:** accounts pay only when the invoice agrees with the PO (what was ordered, at what price) and the GRN (what actually arrived). This catches wrong prices, short deliveries and charges for goods that never came.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In a well-run business, the person who asks for goods, the person who approves the order, the person who receives the goods and the person who pays are not all the same person. This **separation of duties** makes honest mistakes easier to catch and fraud harder. In a small shop one person may do several of these jobs, but the approval and the payment should still be checked by someone else.

Each person may sign orders only up to a set value: their **approval limit** (spending limit). An order above it goes to a more senior person and, in a public body, through more quotations or a tender. Never split one need into smaller orders to keep each under a limit. Even if the price is good, it gets round the controls the limit exists for.

ul: Every PO has its own number, in sequence, and is filed with the requisition, the quotes, the scoring sheet and the approvals.
Ordering through a supplier's website or the Centre's online system keeps the same controls: orders are still approved before they are sent, and still numbered and recorded.
Each person has their own login and password. Passwords are never shared, so every order can be traced to the person who placed it.
Payments by card or bank transfer are approved and checked against statements, like any other payment.

blocks.note: A purchase you cannot explain later, with papers, is a bad purchase even if the steel was right. Ask yourself: could an auditor follow this order from the requisition to the payment without asking me anything?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The **specification** tells the supplier exactly what you need. Write it with the supervisor or engineer, from the drawings, the welding procedure specification (WPS) and the job's standard. Never leave it to the supplier's salesperson: a vague order such as "steel plate, thin" invites the cheapest item that fits the words.

Example
Why it matters

The parts fit and waste is low
The right amount arrives and the unit price is clear
Stainless 2B or No. 4 finish; plate free from heavy pitting; bare or primed

Each piece can be linked to its certificate

Keeps out moisture; protects the finish in handling

head: Material
What the order must say
Points to know
rows: Grade and standard, thickness, sheet size or section size, length
Much of the steel sold in Jamaica is made to American (ASTM) standards, some to British, European or other standards. The drawing names the grade: never substitute without approval.
Hollow sections and pipe (SHS, RHS, CHS)
Size, wall thickness, grade and standard. For pipe: nominal size with the schedule or wall thickness
"2-inch pipe" is a nominal size. Without the schedule (for example Sch 40) or the wall thickness, the order is incomplete.
Grade (304, 304L, 316, 316L), thickness, sheet size, finish (2B mill finish, No. 4 brushed), protective film
316 contains molybdenum and resists salt water and chlorides better than 304: choose it for coastal, marine and fish or brine work
The "L" grades have low carbon and are preferred for welding, as they resist corrosion beside the weld
430 is cheaper but rusts more easily and is harder to weld
Alloy and temper, for example 5052-H32 sheet or 6061-T6 plate and extrusions; size; finish
Alloy and temper decide strength and how it welds. Welding softens heat-treated tempers such as T6 beside the weld, which the designer must allow for.
Diameter and thread (for example M20), length, strength grade (8.8, 10.9), nuts and washers, finish (black, zinc-plated, hot-dip galvanised), standard
A lower grade than the drawing gives a weak joint. Galvanised bolts need nuts made to suit the thicker coating.
The exact class named on the WPS (for example E7018 or ER70S-6), diameter, pack size, batch certificates when the job needs them
A different class can make the WPS invalid. Ask for sealed packs for low-hydrogen electrodes.
Gas or mixture (argon, argon–CO2 mix and its percentages), cylinder size, rental and return terms
The wrong mixture changes the arc and the weld.
The system in the specification: primer, number of coats, colour, dry film thickness
Mixing systems from different makers can cause the coating to fail.

blocks.note: Salt air attacks steel quickly along Jamaica's coasts, from Kingston Harbour to Montego Bay and the whole north coast. Where the drawing calls for galvanising or 316 stainless, do not let a supplier talk you into a cheaper substitute without the engineer's written approval.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **mill certificate** (mill test certificate) is the steel maker's record for one **heat** (one melt) of steel: its chemical analysis and its mechanical test results, such as yield strength, tensile strength and elongation. On a coded job, such as pressure pipe or structural steel built to a code, the order must ask for certificates that give the **actual test results for that heat**. A sales brochure or a sheet of "typical properties" is not enough. In the European system these are called type 3.1 inspection certificates, while a type 2.2 report gives only typical results; ask for the type the job's specification names.

When the steel arrives, the heat number stamped or painted on each piece must match a certificate. If it does not, the steel is put on hold, not used and not re-marked, until the right certificate is obtained.

blocks.note: Before you send an RFQ, read your own specification as if you were a supplier who wanted to send the cheapest thing possible. Every gap you find is a gap a supplier could use.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Send the **same** specification, quantities, delivery date and closing date to every supplier, so the quotes can be compared fairly.

Ask each supplier to show the unit price and total, GCT separately, the delivery charge and lead time, how long the price is valid, payment terms, and any charges for cutting, certificates or handling.
Send it to the number of approved suppliers the rules require (often at least three).
If one supplier asks a question that changes or explains the specification, send the answer to all of them.
Keep every quote confidential, before and after the closing date.

blocks.p: The lowest unit price is not always the lowest cost. Bring every quote to the same basis first: the same items and quantity, with delivery, cutting and other charges added, and GCT treated the same way in each. Then check the lead time against the date the goods are needed and the **validity** (how long the price holds) against the date the order can be approved.

Supplier B has the lowest unit price but the highest total. Supplier C is cheapest overall, but its price lapses after 7 days, so the order must be approved quickly or the validity extended in writing.
When quality, delivery and service matter as well as price, use a **weighted scoring sheet**:

flow: Choose the criteria that matter for this job, such as price, quality, delivery and service
Give each a weight so that the weights add up to 100%, and agree them with the manager BEFORE any quote is opened
Score each supplier out of 10 on each criterion, from its quote and its past records
Multiply each score by its weight written as a decimal (35% = 0.35)
Add the results to get a total out of 10 for each supplier
File the sheet, with the reasons for each score, with the purchase order

blocks.p: Supplier A wins, although C is the cheapest. A common way to score price is to give the lowest total 10 and score the others in proportion; whatever method you use, write it on the sheet before the quotes are opened.

blocks.note: Agree the weights before you open the quotes. Weights chosen after you have seen the prices can be bent, even without meaning to, towards the supplier you already like. And never change a score afterwards to make the result come out the way you wanted.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: An **approved supplier list** holds firms that have been checked: they supply the right grades with proper certificates, deliver reliably and deal fairly.

Keep an approved **second supplier** for key items such as structural steel, argon and low-hydrogen electrodes, so work can carry on if the main supplier runs out, has a breakdown, or is cut off by a storm or a port delay.
Review the list regularly, using the performance records below.

head: Measure
How to work it out
Example
rows: Orders complete and correct ÷ all orders × 100
Count of missing or wrong certificates
Days taken to replace goods or issue a credit

blocks.p: Review the figures every few months. When a supplier slips, gather the facts, meet the supplier, show the figures and agree a plan with dates. Keep the second supplier ready meanwhile. If nothing improves, report to the manager; the supplier may be taken off the approved list.

head: The buyer must
The buyer must not
rows: Give every supplier the same information and the same closing date
Tell one supplier another's price, or hint at it
Split an order to keep it under an approval limit
Declare any link with a supplier (a relative, a friend, a share in the firm) and step back from that decision

Record the reasons for every choice

Pay suppliers on time, as agreed

Buy for private use through the firm's account

blocks.p: HEART/NSTA Trust centres, schools, ministries and municipal corporations spend public money. The **procurement rules for public bodies** require them to buy openly, fairly and competitively, for good value, and to record each step so that an auditor can check it later. The method depends on the value: small purchases need a few written quotations, larger ones a **tender**. The Centre's procurement officer knows the value limits and the forms, so speak to them before you start.
A **tender** is a formal process in which suppliers send sealed prices by a fixed closing date and time, and the bids are judged on criteria stated in advance.

flow: Write a clear, neutral specification: describe what is needed, not a brand (if a brand must be named, add "or equivalent")
Issue the invitation to tender to all eligible suppliers, with the closing date and time, the criteria and their weights
Answer any question from a bidder to all bidders
Keep sealed bids secure and unopened until the closing time
Open all bids together after the closing time, in front of witnesses, and record each price at once
Record late bids as late and return them unopened
Judge the bids only on the stated criteria and weights
Award the contract, tell the unsuccessful bidders, and file every record

blocks.note: Anyone on the evaluation panel who is linked to a bidder must declare it in writing and step back. A fair decision made by someone with a hidden link still looks unfair, and can be overturned.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Negotiation** is the talk in which a buyer and a supplier agree price and terms that suit both sides. Do it honestly: a supplier you deceive will not help you when you need a rush order.

head: Fair ways to get a better deal
Unfair or dishonest tactics
rows: Ask for a volume discount on a large or combined order
Claim to have a lower quote that you do not have
Offer a blanket order for the year in return for fixed prices
Promise future work you do not intend to give
Ask for free delivery, free cutting to length or a longer validity
Threaten to report or bad-mouth the firm
Offer prompt payment in return for a discount
Use one supplier's confidential price to bargain with another
Combine orders from several jobs to reach a price break
Hold back payment that is due, to squeeze a better price

ul: Prepare: know your budget, the usual market price, what you can offer, and the lowest terms you will accept.
Listen to the supplier's costs and limits; look for terms that help both sides, such as a delivery day that suits the supplier's truck.
Write down what is agreed and put it in the purchase order.

blocks.h: Contract terms on the purchase order

head: Term
What it does
rows: The agreed price, and how long it holds
When and where; whether part deliveries are allowed
The supplier pays an agreed sum for each day or week of delay, up to a limit (often called liquidated damages), so the supplier shares the cost of a delay it causes
Goods must meet the specification; the buyer may reject and return goods that do not
Certificates, packing list and delivery note required with the goods; no payment until they are received
For example net 30 days, with any prompt-payment discount
For equipment: how long, what is covered, who repairs it locally
When the goods become the buyer's and who bears loss in transit; for imports, set by the shipping term (FOB, CIF and so on)

sections.title: Buying well: quantities, prices and methods

ul: 1 tonne (t) = 1000 kg. To change kilograms to tonnes, divide by 1000: 2 750 kg = 2.75 t.
Cost = price per tonne × tonnes: J$192 000 per tonne × 2.75 t = J$528 000.
Price per kg = total cost ÷ kilograms.
Mass of plate = length × width × thickness (all in metres) × 7850 kg/m³ (the density of steel). Section masses (kg per metre) come from the supplier's tables.

blocks.p: Suppliers often charge less per unit for larger quantities. Work out the **total** both ways, and ask whether the extra items will be used.
Here 25 discs cost J$65 less than 22, and the shop uses discs every day, so buy 25. But if the item is special to one job, or the higher quantity costs more in total, buy only what is needed.

Primers, two-pack paints, sealants, some fluxes and batteries have a shelf life. A big discount is no saving if half the stock expires before it is used. Buy what will be used within its life, and issue the oldest stock first (first in, first out).
For items used on every job, such as discs, wire, electrodes and gas, the store sets two levels:

ul: **Minimum (reorder) level:** enough to last through the supplier's lead time, plus a safety stock. Example: use 4 packs a day, lead time 5 days, safety stock 6 packs: reorder level = 4 × 5 + 6 = 26 packs.
**Maximum level:** the most that should be held, because of space, cash and shelf life.
When stock falls to the minimum, order enough to bring it back to the maximum. With a maximum of 80 and 24 in stock, order 80 − 24 = 56. (Some stores also add what will be used during the lead time.)

blocks.p: The **economic order quantity** is the order size that keeps the total of ordering costs and holding costs lowest over a year. Ordering often in small amounts costs more in paperwork and deliveries; ordering rarely in large amounts ties up cash and space.
**EOQ = √(2 × D × S ÷ H)**, where D is the yearly usage, S is the cost of placing one order (J$) and H is the cost of holding one item in stock for a year (J$).

head: Worked example: MIG wire spools
Figure
rows: Cost of holding one spool for a year (H)
**60 spools** per order, about 8 orders a year

blocks.note: EOQ assumes steady use and steady prices. It ignores price breaks, shelf life, storage space, cash, and supply shocks such as hurricanes or port delays. Use it as a guide, then use your judgement.
blocks.label: Remember

How it works
Best for
Watch out for

Special items for one job, such as 316L pipe or a special flux
Time and paperwork if used for everyday items
Prices and terms agreed with one supplier for a period, often a year; quantities are called off as needed
Items used every week: discs, wire, E7018, gas
Track the total called off against the approved value; check prices on every invoice
The supplier's stock is kept in your store; you pay only for what you take out
Careful counting; a written agreement on who carries loss or damage
Approved suppliers and rates fixed for a period; orders placed as needed
Public bodies; services such as galvanising, cylinder rental, transport
Orders must still be approved and recorded
Small, urgent items bought on the spot

blocks.p: A **make-or-buy decision** compares the full cost of making a part in the shop with the full cost of buying it in, and then weighs quality, accuracy, skills, equipment, workload and time.

head: 60 gusset plates with holes
Make in the shop
Buy laser-cut
rows: Time to prepare drawing files and check parts on arrival
Shop already busy; holes drilled by hand
Accurate, identical parts; frees welders for welding

blocks.p: A service such as galvanising, laser cutting, machining, painting, testing, transport or crane hire is bought with a PO, just like goods. The PO must describe the work exactly: the items and quantities with their drawings and piece marks; the result or standard required (for galvanising, the coating standard and minimum thickness); the inspections, tests and certificates; delivery and collection; the price and terms; and any special warnings.

blocks.note: Hot-dip galvanising dips steel into molten zinc at about 450 °C. Air or water trapped inside a closed hollow section expands violently and can burst the part and throw molten zinc at the galvaniser's workers. Hollow sections need vent and drain holes, sized and placed as the galvaniser advises, and the galvaniser must be told about them before the steel is sent. Remove welding slag, paint and marker paint first: the galvaniser's acid cleaning does not remove them and they leave bare spots.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Define the need:** the processes (MMAW, GMAW, FCAW, GTAW), the current range and duty cycle needed, and whether the machine must be portable.

**Check the supply:** Jamaica's mains are 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz. The machine must suit the supply where it will be used, single-phase or three-phase, and the Centre's electrician confirms that the circuit can carry its input current.
**Write a neutral specification** that describes performance, not a brand.
**Compare whole-life cost,** not just price: accessories, consumables, power, servicing, spare parts held in Jamaica, warranty, training, and how long the machine will last.

**Accept it properly:** check it against the PO, make sure the manuals and warranty papers are there, have it installed and tested by competent people, then sign for it and add it to the equipment register with its serial number and service dates.

Before ordering a large number of gas cylinders, check that the store has approved, ventilated, shaded space to keep them upright and chained, with oxygen apart from fuel gases, and agree the rental and return terms.
Order flammable paints and thinners only in amounts the fire-safe store can hold.
Ask for the safety data sheet (SDS) with the first delivery of any chemical, and file it.

blocks.p: Some items are not stocked in Jamaica in the grade, size, finish or quantity a job needs: 316L sheet in a special finish, large pipe, special consumables. The buyer then imports, directly or through a local agent. Importing takes longer, needs more paperwork and carries costs that do not show in the overseas price.

An overseas price always comes with a **shipping term** that says where the seller's costs and risks end and the buyer's begin. These terms are the Incoterms rules, published by the International Chamber of Commerce. Always write the term and the named place, such as "FOB Miami" or "CIF Kingston".

head: Term
Stands for
The seller pays
The buyer pays
rows: Only to have the goods ready at its own premises
Everything from there: loading, export, freight, insurance, import costs
FOB (named port of shipment), e.g. FOB Miami
All costs until the goods are loaded on board the ship at that port
Sea freight, insurance, unloading, duty, fees, GCT, broker, port charges and haulage
CIF (named port of destination), e.g. CIF Kingston
The goods, sea freight and basic insurance to that port
Unloading and port charges, duty, fees, GCT, broker and haulage
Delivered At Place / Delivered Duty Paid
Delivery to the named place; with DDP, import duties too
With DAP, the import duties and fees; with DDP, very little

blocks.note: With FOB and CIF, the risk of loss passes to the buyer once the goods are on board at the port of shipment, even though under CIF the seller pays the freight and buys the insurance. CIF insurance is usually the minimum cover, so ask whether more is needed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **landed cost** is the full cost of getting the goods to your gate. Only the landed cost can be compared fairly with a local supplier's delivered price.

flow: Overseas price, converted to J$
+ sea freight and insurance (if the price is FOB)
+ customs duty and other import charges and fees
+ GCT at the current rate (the Centre's accounts office says whether it can be claimed back)
+ customs broker's fee and port and handling charges
+ haulage from the port to the workshop
= landed cost

head: Worked example (made-up figures): 316L sheet
Amount
rows: Duty and fees (as the broker estimates)

blocks.p: A local supplier quotes J$1 545 000 delivered, before GCT. The import looks J$53 900 cheaper, but it takes about nine weeks and carries exchange-rate risk: if the rate moves from J$156 to J$162 before payment, the US$7 835 costs 7 835 × 6 = J$47 010 more, and the saving shrinks to J$6 890. The local supplier may then be the better buy.

ul: Rates are written as J$ per US$1. **US$ to J$: multiply** by the rate. **J$ to US$: divide** by the rate.
Rates move. If you pay weeks or months after ordering, the J$ cost may rise. Allow a margin in the budget, or ask accounts whether to buy the US dollars when the order is placed.
The rate a bank sells you US dollars at is higher than the rate it buys them at. Use the selling rate for your estimate.

blocks.p: A licensed **customs broker** knows the forms, the tariff codes and the customs process. The broker lodges the declaration, arranges payment of the duty and fees, and gets the goods released. Most fabrication shops use one, and the broker's fee is part of the landed cost. The broker does not pay your duty for you or make the goods cheaper.
Work back from the date the materials must be in the workshop, adding every stage and a margin for delays.

Total: needed in week 15, so order by week 6

blocks.note: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. Storms can close ports and delay sailings in Florida and Jamaica for days. In these months order earlier, allow a bigger margin, and do not plan for goods to land just before they are needed.
blocks.label: Jamaica

Control

Late shipping, missed sailing, port congestion
Order early; margin in the timeline; track the shipment; expedite
Avoid tight dates in the season; approved second supplier; insurance
Clear specification; certificates and photos before shipping; check on arrival

Missing documents hold the goods at the port while storage charges build up
Document checklist; copies in hand before the ship arrives
Ask the broker to estimate duty and fees before ordering

blocks.p: **Expediting** means checking that an order will arrive on time, and chasing it if not. Do not wait for the due date to find out it is late.

ul: When the order acknowledgement comes, check it against the PO: items, sizes, quantities, price, date.
Put a check in your diary a few days before the due date and confirm the goods have been dispatched. For an import, check at each stage: made, shipped, arrived at port, cleared.
If an order will be late, get a firm new date in writing, tell the supervisor so the work can be re-planned, and consider the second supplier.
Record late deliveries for the supplier's performance review, and apply the late delivery clause if the order has one.

blocks.p: Once a PO is placed, the money is **committed**: it is promised to the supplier even though no invoice has come. The job budget must count committed costs as well as amounts already paid, or it looks healthier than it is.

ul: The storekeeper checks the goods against the PO and the delivery note: items, sizes, grades, quantities.
Condition: bends, rust pitting, damaged coatings, laminations (layers in the plate that show at cut edges), wet or torn consumable packs.
Certificates: every heat number on the steel matches a certificate with the actual results; consumable batch certificates are there if ordered.
Shortages and damage are written on the delivery note before it is signed, and on the goods received note.
A delivery that matches no order is held to one side until purchasing has checked it.

flow: Set the faulty goods apart and label them HOLD or REJECTED
Photograph and measure the fault
Report to the buyer at once
The buyer tells the supplier in writing, quoting the PO and the fault
Agree a replacement or a credit, and return the goods as agreed
The buyer raises a debit note; the supplier issues a credit note
Record the problem in the supplier's performance file

blocks.note: Never hide or use faulty steel to keep a job moving. Laminated plate, the wrong grade or uncertified steel can make welds fail in service, and once welded in, the claim against the supplier is lost.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Pay only after the three-way match: invoice, PO and GRN agree. Query any difference before paying.
**Net 30** means the full amount is due within 30 days of the invoice date.

**2/10, net 30** means 2% off if paid within 10 days; otherwise the full amount by day 30. Example: an invoice of J$86 500 paid on day 7: 2% of J$86 500 = J$1 730, so pay J$84 770. Paid on day 15, the full J$86 500 is due.
A 2% discount for paying 20 days early is worth a great deal over a year: take it when cash allows.
Suppliers who are paid on time give better prices, credit and help with rush orders.

blocks.p: After the job, ask: was the right thing bought, at the right total cost, on time? Record each supplier's delivery, quality and certificate performance, note what to do differently next time, and file all the papers with the job.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section.

ul: I can describe the purchasing cycle from the requisition to the supplier review, and name the document and the owner of each step.
I can explain approval limits, separation of duties and the three-way match, and why orders must never be split.
I can write a full specification for steel, stainless, aluminium, bolts, consumables and gas, and say why each part matters.
I can explain what a mill certificate with actual results is, and what to do when the heat numbers or certificates are wrong.
I can send a fair RFQ and compare quotes on total cost, lead time and validity.
I can set up a weighted scoring sheet, with weights agreed in advance, and work out the scores.
I can measure supplier performance with on-time and reject rates, and act on poor performance.
I can explain the buyer's duties in a tender for a public body, and deal with conflicts of interest, gifts and late bids.
I can negotiate fairly and name tactics that are dishonest.
I can work out price breaks, costs per tonne and per kg, minimum and maximum stock orders, and the EOQ.
I can choose between one-off orders, blanket orders, consignment stock and term contracts.
I can make a make-or-buy comparison, and write a PO for a service such as galvanising.
I can plan the purchase of a welding machine on whole-life cost and check it suits Jamaica's supply.
I can explain FOB and CIF, work out a landed cost in J$, and allow for exchange-rate risk.
I can list the import documents and plan an import timeline with a margin, allowing for the hurricane season.
I can expedite an order, count committed costs, deal with rejects, and pay correctly on terms such as 2/10, net 30.

terms: Approval limit
The highest order value a person is allowed to approve
Bill of lading
The shipping line's receipt and contract for goods loaded on a ship; needed to collect them at the port
Blanket order
An order that fixes prices and terms with one supplier for a period, with quantities called off as needed
Call-off
A request for a delivery under a blanket order
CIF
Cost, insurance and freight: the seller pays the goods, freight and basic insurance to the named port
Commercial invoice
The seller's invoice for exported goods; customs use it to assess duty
Committed cost
Money promised to suppliers by orders placed but not yet invoiced
Consignment stock
The supplier's stock kept in the buyer's store; paid for only when used
Credit note
A supplier's document reducing the amount the buyer owes
Customs broker
A licensed agent who clears imported goods through customs
Debit note
A buyer's document telling the supplier it is reducing the amount owed, for example for returned goods
EOQ
Economic order quantity: the order size that keeps ordering and holding costs lowest
Expediting
Checking that an order will arrive on time, and chasing it
FOB
Free on board: the seller's costs end when the goods are loaded on the ship at the named port
Goods received note (GRN)
The store's record of what arrived and its condition
Heat number
The number that identifies one melt of steel and links each piece to its mill certificate
Incoterms
The international rules that set out shipping terms such as FOB and CIF
Landed cost
The full cost of getting imported goods to your gate
Liquidated damages
An agreed sum the supplier pays for each day or week of late delivery
Make or buy
The choice between making a part in the shop and buying it in
Mill certificate
The steel maker's record of the chemical and test results for one heat of steel
Negotiation
The talks in which buyer and supplier agree price and terms
Packing list
The list of what is in each crate, bundle or pallet of a shipment
Price break
A lower unit price for buying a larger quantity
Purchase order (PO)
The buyer's numbered, approved order to a supplier
Purchase requisition
A request, approved by the budget holder, for goods to be bought
RFQ
Request for quotation: asks suppliers to price the same specification by the same date
Specification
The exact description of what is to be bought
Tender
A formal process in which suppliers send sealed bids by a closing date, judged on stated criteria
Three-way match
Checking that the invoice agrees with the purchase order and the goods received note before paying
Validity
How long a quoted price holds
Weighted scoring
Scoring suppliers on several criteria, each multiplied by an agreed weight

c1.title: Handrail pipe for a clinic in Linstead
c1.text: Marlon Campbell buys materials for a fabrication shop in Linstead, St Catherine. For the handrails and ramp at a health clinic he needs 40 lengths of 1½-inch Sch 40 galvanised pipe, 6 m long. He sent the same request for quotation to three approved suppliers, closing at noon on Friday. Supplier P quotes J$9 800 a length with free delivery in 4 days. Supplier Q quotes J$9 200 a length plus J$31 000 delivery, in 6 days. Supplier R quotes J$9 500 a length plus J$8 000 delivery, in 3 days, with the price valid for 5 days only. The scoring sheet, agreed with the manager before the quotes came in, weights price 45%, quality 35% and delivery 20%.

c2.title: Stainless tables for a fish plant in Whitehouse
c2.text: Shernette Wint is the buyer for a shop in Whitehouse, Westmoreland, that is making cleaning tables and wash troughs for a fish-processing plant. The tables will be washed down with salty water every day. The sheet is not stocked locally in the size needed, so Shernette has an overseas quote of US$7 400 FOB Miami. Freight to Kingston is US$1 100 and insurance US$100. For this case, use J$158 to US$1. The customs broker estimates duty and fees at J$190 000; the broker's fee is J$32 000, port charges J$26 000 and haulage from Kingston to Whitehouse J$38 000. The plant wants the tables installed by mid-October.

c3.title: The workshop store in Old Harbour
c3.text: Kerry-Ann Henry runs the welding workshop store at a training centre in Old Harbour, St Catherine. The workshop uses about 2 500 flap discs a year. Placing and processing one order costs the Centre about J$1 800, and holding one disc in stock for a year costs about J$36. Argon is bought on a blanket order approved at J$600 000 for the financial year; by October the call-offs already total J$560 000, and the busiest term is still to come. A wire supplier has offered to keep a stock of MIG wire and E7018 electrodes in the Centre's store and bill only for what is taken out.

c4.title: A steel tender in Brown's Town
c4.text: A training centre in Brown's Town, St Ann, which is a public body, is buying about 18 tonnes of steel hollow section for a training project: market stall frames for the municipal corporation. Because of the value, the procurement officer is running a tender that closes at 10:00 a.m. on a set Tuesday. Mr Dujon Clarke, the workshop supervisor, is on the evaluation panel; his cousin owns one of the firms likely to bid. The first draft of the specification, written by a trainee, names one maker's brand of tubing. On the closing day, one bidder's sealed envelope is handed in at 10:25 a.m.

c5.title: Late plate for water tanks in Christiana
c5.text: Tavia Morgan buys steel for a shop in Christiana, Manchester, that builds water tanks to a code. Purchase order 2214 was for 24 sheets of 8 mm plate, with mill certificates giving the actual test results for each heat, due on a Monday. Tavia did not contact the supplier after sending the order, and the truck arrived on Thursday. Six sheets had deep rust pitting and were sent back; the supplier agreed to credit them. The corrected invoice is J$612 000, on terms of 2/10, net 30. Tavia's records show this supplier made 25 deliveries this year, of which 22 were on time.

questions.q: Before GCT, which supplier gives the lowest total cost for the 40 lengths?
o: Supplier R, at J$388 000
Supplier Q, at J$368 000
Supplier P, at J$392 000
Supplier Q, at J$399 000
questions.why: Compare totals, not unit prices: P is 40 × J$9 800 = J$392 000; Q is J$368 000 + J$31 000 = J$399 000; R is J$380 000 + J$8 000 = J$388 000. Q's low unit price hides a high delivery charge.

questions.q: The manager cannot approve the order until next Wednesday, six days after the quotes close. What does this mean for Supplier R's quote?
o: R must still supply at the quoted price, as it is in writing
Its price will have lapsed, so ask R in writing to extend it
R must now be scored zero for price, as the quote has expired
The order should go to R at once, before the manager approves it
questions.why: A quoted price holds only for its validity period; after that the supplier may change it. Ask R before the deadline to extend the validity in writing, so the comparison stays fair. An order is never placed before it is approved.

questions.q: Supplier R scores 9 for price, 6 for quality and 9 for delivery. Marlon's assistant adds the three scores, divides by 3 and gets 8.0. What is wrong?
o: Nothing: a plain average is fair to all three suppliers
He should have added the scores, giving R a total of 24
He should have used price alone, which gives R a 9
He ignored the weights; the sheet gives R 7.95
questions.why: Each score is multiplied by its weight: 9 × 0.45 + 6 × 0.35 + 9 × 0.20 = 4.05 + 2.10 + 1.80 = 7.95. A plain average treats quality as worth no more than delivery, which is not what the manager agreed.

questions.q: On the same sheet P scores 8, 9 and 7, a total of 8.15, so P beats R even though R is cheaper. What should Marlon do next?
o: Change the weights so that the cheaper supplier comes out on top
Order from R anyway, as the lowest price must always win
File the sheet and reasons, and recommend P for approval
Lower P's quality score so the two suppliers come out level
questions.why: P's total is 8 × 0.45 + 9 × 0.35 + 7 × 0.20 = 8.15. The weights were agreed before the quotes were opened, so the result stands; a higher price can be the better buy when quality matters, and the filed sheet lets anyone check the decision.

questions.q: Which stainless grade should Shernette's specification name for these tables?
o: 304, as it is the most common grade for food work
316, which resists salt water better than 304
430, as it is cheaper and is still a stainless steel
Any grade, as long as the No. 4 finish is given
questions.why: Salt (chloride) attacks stainless steel by pitting. 316 contains molybdenum, which gives it much better resistance than 304; 316L is its low-carbon form for welding. The finish matters too, but it does not change the grade.

questions.q: What is the landed cost of the sheet in J$, before GCT?
questions.why: FOB means the buyer pays freight and insurance: US$7 400 + US$1 100 + US$100 = US$8 600 × 158 = J$1 358 800. Adding duty and fees (J$190 000), the broker (J$32 000), port charges (J$26 000) and haulage (J$38 000) gives J$1 644 800.

questions.q: By the time the supplier is paid, the rate has moved to J$163 to US$1. How much more will the US$8 600 cost in J$?
questions.why: Each US dollar now costs J$5 more: US$8 600 × 5 = J$43 000. This is why an import budget carries a margin for exchange-rate movement, or the dollars are bought when the order is placed.

questions.q: The tables must be installed by mid-October. What does this mean for Shernette's import plan?
o: Plan for the sheet to land just before it is needed, to save space
Ship it by air, as sea freight always takes three months or more
Order early and allow a wider margin, as it is hurricane season
Nothing special: sea freight times are the same all year round
questions.why: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November, and storms can close ports and delay sailings. Work back from the date the sheet is needed and add a bigger margin for delays in these months.

questions.q: Using EOQ = √(2 × D × S ÷ H), what is the economic order quantity for the flap discs?
o: 354 discs
250 discs
1 000 discs
500 discs
questions.why: 2 × 2 500 × 1 800 = 9 000 000; ÷ 36 = 250 000; √250 000 = 500. Ordering 500 at a time means about five orders a year, which keeps ordering and holding costs together at their lowest.

questions.q: What should Kerry-Ann do about the argon blanket order?
o: Keep calling off cylinders until the supplier refuses to send more
Switch to petty cash purchases for the rest of the financial year
Warn purchasing now, so the order can be raised or renewed
Ask the supplier to put the next cylinders on a separate account
questions.why: A blanket order has an approved total value, and spending past it without approval breaks the controls. Warn purchasing early, with the expected use, so an increase or a new order is approved in time.

questions.q: Before the Centre accepts the consignment stock offer, what must be agreed in writing?
o: That the Centre pays for all the stock when it is delivered
That the stock stays at the supplier's yard until it is needed
How the stock is counted and who carries any loss
That the Centre need not count or record what it takes
questions.why: Consignment stock belongs to the supplier until it is taken out and used. Both sides must agree how withdrawals are recorded, how often stock is counted, and who pays if stock is damaged, spoiled or stolen.

questions.q: What is wrong with the first draft of the specification?
o: Nothing: naming a brand makes the order clearer for every bidder
It favours one maker; it should state grade, sizes and standard
It should name two brands, so that there is some competition
It should leave out the sizes, so suppliers can offer their own
questions.why: A tender specification describes what is needed, not who makes it, so that every qualified supplier can bid. If a brand must be mentioned, it is followed by "or equivalent".

questions.q: What should Mr Clarke do about his cousin's firm?
o: Stay on the panel but give his cousin's bid an average score
Declare the link in writing and step back from the panel
Ask his cousin not to bid this time, then stay on the panel
Say nothing, as long as he scores every bid honestly
questions.why: A conflict of interest must be declared and the person must step back from the decision. Even an honest score looks unfair if the link is hidden, and the procurement rules for public bodies require it to be declared.

questions.q: What should happen to the envelope handed in at 10:25 a.m.?
o: Record it as late and return it unopened
Open it with the others, as 25 minutes late is close enough
Open it first, to see whether it holds the cheapest price
Accept it if the bidder phones to explain the delay
questions.why: Late bids are refused so that no bidder can gain an advantage, for example by learning about the others. Recording the time and returning the bid unopened shows an auditor that the rules were kept.

questions.q: Why are the bids opened together after the closing time, in front of witnesses, with each price recorded at once?
o: So bidders can lower their prices once they hear the others
So the winner can be chosen on price alone, there and then
So the bids can be opened faster than one at a time
So no bid can be altered or lost, and an audit can check it
questions.why: Opening bids together, witnessed and recorded on the spot, protects both the public body and the bidders. The bids are then judged on the criteria and weights stated in the tender, not on price alone.

questions.q: The shop expects approved suppliers to deliver at least 90% of orders on time. How does this supplier compare?
o: Above it, at 92%
Below it, at 88%
Exactly on it, at 90%
Far below it, at 22%
questions.why: 22 on time out of 25 is 22 ÷ 25 × 100 = 88%, just under the target. One figure alone is no reason to drop a supplier, but it is a reason to raise the problem with the facts and agree how it will improve.

questions.q: The corrected invoice is paid 6 days after the invoice date. How much should be paid?
questions.why: "2/10, net 30" gives 2% off if paid within 10 days: 2% of J$612 000 is J$12 240, so J$599 760 is paid. After day 10 the full amount is due by day 30.

questions.q: What should Tavia have done after sending the order, so the late delivery did not take the shop by surprise?
o: Checked the acknowledgement and chased it before the due date
Waited, as chasing a supplier before the due date annoys them
Phoned the supplier every morning from the day she sent the order
Paid the invoice early so the supplier would deliver on time
questions.why: Expediting starts with checking that the order acknowledgement matches the PO, then confirming dispatch a few days before the due date. Finding a slip early gives time to re-plan the work or use a second supplier.

questions.q: With the plate, the supplier sends a sheet of "typical properties" for the grade instead of the heat certificates. What should Tavia do?
o: Accept it, as typical values show what the grade should achieve
Use the plate on parts the inspector is unlikely to look at
Ask the welders to bend an offcut in the vice to test it
Hold the plate and ask for each heat's certificate
questions.why: On a coded job the inspector must see the real test results for the heat each plate came from. Typical values prove nothing about this plate, so it stays on hold until the right certificates arrive.

questions.q: A shop needs 9 spools of 316L stainless MIG wire for one job and rarely uses this wire. Spools cost J$7 900 each for 1–9, or J$7 300 each for 10 or more. What should the buyer do?
o: Buy 9 for J$71 100; 10 would cost J$73 000
Buy 10, as the lower unit price always saves money
Buy 9 at J$7 300 each, J$65 700 in all
Buy 10 and send the spare back after the job
questions.why: Ten spools cost 10 × J$7 300 = J$73 000, more than 9 × J$7 900 = J$71 100, and the spare would sit unused. A price break is worth taking only when the total is lower or the extra will really be used.
